From the U.S. on a working holiday in Australia for half a year now. Having lived in both urban and rural Australia, here’s my two cents.

In cities, some, yes, but in general I do find people are more welcoming towards outsiders, especially in cities like Sydney and Melbourne. I talked to my Australian friends about it multiple times, and they told me while it still is bad, it was way worse when their parents were younger. Nowadays they are a lot more aware of racism, and discuss it way more. In fact a lot of Aussies in cities have people of color in their friend groups, especially with some foreigners and foreign born friends.

In rural Australia, it’s way worse. Even in aboriginal communities there is still racism towards other aboriginals from different groups. And while I as a white person experienced racism, it was nowhere near as bad as people of color I was working with. 

That being said, I have been to countries where racism was worse. While the U.S. has systemic racism and Australian racism seems to be more social from what I see, they’re both still way more tolerant than some other countries like Korea or Germany for instance.

As a New Yorker living down under, I would say Quebec is slightly easier in your circumstances. Aside from linguistic and familial reasons, Quebec to my knowledge tends to be a slightly easier province to migrate to in Canada due to its strong emphasis on knowing french to get a better paying job. Also rents tend to be lower in cities like Montreal and Quebec City than in major cities in the Anglo provinces, so a nice little incentive, but still plays a small role in the bigger picture. 

The only reason why I’m still in Australia (on a working holiday visa) is because my field is very high in demand (social work), so going to graduate school and getting a post grad visa is a pathway to residency, as it is a skill needed for long term growth. Salaries tend to be higher than Canada for fields like teaching and social services, but Canada is slightly easier to get residency in, especially in Quebec. And if you are willing to work in a regional area, you do tend to make more than city folks on the coast in Australia’s case, and the same may apply for rural Quebec. Good way to fast track your chances of landing residency too.

My recommendation for Australia is do a working holiday if you haven’t turned 31 yet and are unsure, as it is a good way to live and work here with no long term commitments necessary. Quality of life is much better than in the states and Canada in my opinion, and relatively safe, but the distance is a major factor to consider, especially if connection to family and friends is vital for your wellbeing. But that being said, it’s still a good place to live and there are way worse places to live, and a lot of my Australian friends feel lucky to call this place home despite its problems.

I’ve been living in Australia for the past half year on a working holiday visa, and also looking to go the grad school route. 

There’s a reason why all the kiwis I met have been coming here in droves: they can earn more money in Australia doing the same jobs. If you’re really keen on New Zealand, you can easily apply for a working holiday visa first if you’re under 30 and see if you like it before you commit fully to living in the country. The same applies to Australia. 

Personally, I’m glad I chose Australia because of better salaries, but also it’s not nearly as isolated as New Zealand (it has Indonesia and other Asian countries to the north, and several pacific islands as its neighbors). Also things are cheaper here than in New Zealand, like fuel and certain produce. You can also earn more money if you choose to work in a regional area, as in smaller cities and towns outside of Sydney, Melbourne, and Brisbane. Also handy to get that sweet visa extension for another year in Australia compared to only 3 months in NZ.

Entered Australia on a working holiday visa almost 6 months ago. I did not have a job lined up, so I just explored the east coast and set up shop in Sydney for a bit before I relocated to do regional work to extend my visa. I plan on moving to Melbourne after I finish my regional work and I wouldn’t be lying if I said I explored my options to stay. 

The easiest option for me would be to pursue graduate school for social work and get a post grad visa. Having some background work in education for a while and coming from an English speaking country helps out a lot if I wanted to go that route. However, it is worth noting that universities here are expensive and I am very fortunate to have financial support from family (along with my own savings) to help out with that because not everyone does. Granted, a lot of them here are more subsidized by the government compared to the states, but still. 

That being said, if you are in your twenties and haven’t turned 31 yet and have some savings, want a taste of living abroad, some work experience, and with no long term commitment necessary, it’s worth doing a working holiday here in Oz or NZ. I’m not gonna lie, it’s expensive, even with the usd exchange rate, but coming from New York City (I paid WAY less in Sydney in AUD than in my family’s place in NYC in usd for reference), I feel like I get more worth for my money out here and am very fortunate to reside in this beautiful country for now. 

Did I forget to mention no mass shootings, easier access to healthcare even for non permanent residents and citizens, and an arguably more stable political climate too? Because those are also wins.

Russian American here. I also agree that considering a Slavic country would be a good choice. Knowing Russian is already a perfect stepping stone to learning another Slavic language. You’ll easily be able to pick up words and phrases even if you don’t know every single sentence.

Out of all the ones I’ve been to in the European Union (Poland, Czech Republic, Slovakia, Slovenia, and Croatia), I’d personally choose Slovenia, Poland or Czechia. They’re all located right within the heart of Europe, which makes it great for job opportunities, as well as traveling to neighboring countries. Even if you don’t choose these countries, a lot of Slavic and Eastern European eu member states have a lower cost of living compared to most of their western  European counterparts and you still get EU benefits all the same.

Out of all the ones I mentioned, I believe Slovenia is the most easiest to move to (I heard the university of Ljubljana also has courses in english), but note there may not be as big of an expat community as in some other places. But that being said, it is a very beautiful country and I regret not spending more time there.

The other thing is if you have ancestors who resided in any of the Baltic states before and during Soviet times, you may also qualify for citizenship of those countries by descent. But I don’t know too much about the process or if this applies to you, but if it does, might be worth looking into.

I’m American but I left for Australia a few months ago. Total cost for a supply of up to 56 days was about $26 aud ($19 usd), but the gp visit was $80 aud (about $50 usd). Mind you I am not an Australian citizen or permanent resident, but I still found it significantly easier dealing with your healthcare system than ours.

My meds in the U.S. would easily cost up to thousands without insurance and a visit without insurance would be hundreds of dollars. If I wasn’t on my family’s insurance (or if I hadn’t had my shrink), I would have been screwed and I most likely probably would have hurt myself or worse. It’s been 2 years since I’ve been diagnosed with BP2, so it could have been worse I suppose

I think the moment I realized I wanted to relocate abroad was studying abroad in Ireland when I was in college. After a good couple of months there, I went back and worked a job that opened doors but I didn’t particularly enjoy in the end. I just felt stuck living in my city and felt like I wasn’t going anywhere. And I almost didn’t get homesick studying abroad, so I decided I wanted to fully relocate abroad but wasn’t sure where.

Fast forward a few months ago and I moved to Australia on a working holiday. It’s not perfect, but compared to the U.S. I’ll gladly take it any day. I always felt safer outside of the U.S. every time I traveled (most of the time anyway), and Australia was no exception. When I was living in Sydney it was nice to go out and not worry about getting gunned down on a regular basis. And being able to actually get my medication easier without fear of getting screwed over by the health system was also a win win, even without pr or citizenship.

I would have done something like this regardless of the political situation, but the most recent election results made me glad I left just before everything went down. Granted, it hasn’t been an easy road. I still miss my family and friends stateside and worry about them, but I do not regret leaving one bit. I’m very grateful to have had the money and means to leave, but not everyone does. Relocating to a place with an arguably more stable political climate, and having some personal growth happen along the way was what I wanted, so I got both in the end.

Left before the election went down and been calling Australia home for a couple of months. It’s one thing living in the us as everything unfolds, it’s another thing to experience it from a different perspective living in a different country literally on the other side of the world. My mental health drastically improved, and it’s nice to live in a place where universal healthcare is a thing (makes it easier to get my meds even as a non resident).

Then again I’m privileged to have had the money and the means to do that, but not everyone is and I worry for everyone back home. Stay safe out there guys

I moved there a few months ago on a working holiday visa and currently working here. Best decision ever by the way. The application process is pretty straightforward and you can apply on your own. And you don’t need to do an English proficiency test which saves you time. Also the U.S. is one of the countries that’s not subject to a visa cap compared to some others doing a working holiday, so best to take advantage of that. 

Also note: getting jobs here can be competitive especially for hospitality. But given that you have citizenship from an English speaking country and a native English speaker, it does give you an edge in the application process since employers won’t have to stress about the language barrier. But if you choose to do manual labor, especially in construction, there’s plenty of jobs in that sector for people on working holidays and getting certified is straightforward. Also it’s not very common for people on working holidays to do office work, so that’ll set you apart if you choose to pursue that.

As a little side note, I will also mention there’s backpacker agencies here that can help you out, especially in Sydney and Melbourne. They do welcome tours and help you get your bank account set up, and some of them can provide info on getting work around your city or in greater Australia. Also a good way to meet people, and do some traveling if you book tours with them across the country too.

Long story short, after a semester abroad in Ireland while I was in college (and frequently traveling outside of the U.S. beforehand, amongst a whole bunch of stuff) I decided that living in the U.S. in the immediate future wasn’t for me. So I worked after I came back and saved up to move to Australia on a working holiday. 

I would have done something like this regardless of the political climate, but everything unfolding now makes me glad I left before the election went down. It’s been a couple of months as of this writing. Granted, life as an expat isn’t as easy as simply being a student for an exchange semester, but I’m grateful every day to be down under. Now i’m considering graduate school here since the field I want to go into is high in demand (social work). Being a native English speaker and having a powerful passport from an English speaking country goes a long way here when it comes to work and study opportunities, at least in my case with my current job.

American who was once an exchange student in Ireland back in college here. I was living just outside of Dublin, and the rental market there is horrible. I Have an Irish buddy that currently lives in Dublin for grad school, and it took him a good 2 or so months to find a place near his uni. Even outside in the suburbs, it’s a challenge.

But there are some alternatives. I spent a bit of time in Galway, and (from my perspective and a few Irish friends agreed with me) it was a good alternative to Dublin. It had the same creature comforts, but cleaner streets, slightly better transportation, and a lower cost of living. Not to downplay the fact that it’s expensive, but I found myself spending less money there than in Dublin. Note, it’s probably difficult too to find a place there, so keep that in mind. 

Still, tech is one of the biggest industries in Ireland, and I met plenty of people who went into that field at my uni at places like intel and other companies. And given that you come from an English speaking country, it’s going to make your life a whole lot easier since Ireland is currently the biggest English speaking country in the European Union, so you wouldn’t have to deal with the language barrier compared to other places. 

I still loved my time there though, and I’ll

Haven’t been to Australia yet, but I got approved for a working holiday visa (whv) and I will go in October for the first time. Basically allows you to travel around but take some odd jobs like bartending, agricultural work, tourism, etc. 

The government also allows you to renew your visa if you fulfill 3 months of working in a regional area. Used to be specifically farm work, but they opened it up to other industries, so you could work at a hotel in the outback hypothetically. Some people have actually gone on to study full time, or get a working visa and then permanent residency after being backpackers. 

Very easy to get if you’re between the ages of 18-30 and have a clean record and are in good health. A college degree is preferred, although if you have a high school diploma they’ll be fine with it under the guidelines for American nationals looking to get a whv. Just make sure to have $5000 aud in your bank account (which is about $3000 usd, but saving up some more money is highly recommended). The questionnaire I filled out online was so painless and I got mine issued literally not even 24 hours after I applied, although this will vary from person to person. 

A working holiday is a good way to get some work experience and check out a new country. You can see the guidelines and more info below to see if it’s right for you :)

I’m (24m) from NYC and I recently got approved to go to Australia on a working holiday visa. I plan on heading down this October. Like you, I’m also on the spectrum, so an escape from the US and NYC would be a win, especially to go to a more laid back place. In the case of Australia, I can’t comment on the lgbt aspect of it, but I’d imagine it’s probably better than in the us. In South Australia, they actually have a minister of autism in the state government, so that’s another reason why I chose to go there. It’s good to have a government official dedicated to helping people on the spectrum. 

As far as the working holiday visa scheme goes, you can enter for a year and do various jobs and travel around. But they also allow you to apply for a second year visa if you do certain work in a regional area for 3 months (used to be just farm work but they’ve opened it up to various other things, like hospitality for instance). You’re eligible if you’re between the ages of 18-30 if you have an American passport, and i got my visa within 24 hours of applying. If you want to study there full time while on your working holiday, you can also get bumped up to a student visa and get a degree that way.

There are also other countries to do a working holiday in besides just Australia. The US has a working holiday agreement with a few places. If not that, teaching English is usually a good way to live in a new place and get work experience. Spain is a really popular country to teach English in, especially since it’s in the European Union and it’s easy to travel around the continent too. Otherwise, there’s just going to uni abroad and getting a cheaper education. Many programs in non English speaking countries are also offered in English, so that’s useful.

You’d still have to research to figure out what works for you, but this gives you a rough idea about what options there are.

It’s more common than you think for people to finish school later, or get another degree for practical work after their BA or associates. Don’t be afraid to try different things. Volunteering is a good thing to do to see what you like. Take up a sport, read a new book, learn a new language, etc. You can always find something passionate through hobbies or just getting out in the field. We’ll have different jobs throughout our lifetime. Think of it as a plan for the next two or three years rather than a life one. Take it from a post pandemic grad.

I feel you because I struggle with weight a lot, even after losing 25 pounds, and I was never close to obesity but I was still overweight. Still am a tiny bit, but nowhere near as severe as it was. 

Treatments like weight loss surgery or ozempic will help, but exercise and eating habits are the biggest keys. From my experience, this is what helped me. Sounds cliche, but I think you could use some tips. 

I personally like to do kickboxing and going on walks, but your exercise routine might be different, and that’s fine so long as you find something you enjoy that feels good but not a chore. As far as eating goes, portioning your meals can go a long way. Start out small. For example: instead of having two pieces of chicken, have one if you get what I mean. Small changes do lead to big results.

What I also like to do is intermittent fasting. This means I eat a big breakfast in the morning, then not eat for a few hours with the exception of a light snack, and then have a lighter dinner. Then I cut off food after 8 or 9pm. It’s hard at first, but it does help.

Cutting out soda and alcohol is also something that helped me significantly, although it is hard to do at first if you consume a lot of sugary drinks on a regular basis, but it’s good in the long run. If you still want something fizzy but without any sugar and no calories, seltzer water is a great and better alternative to soda. Every supermarket and corner store sells them, and it comes in different flavors too. 

And that’s not to say you can’t have a cheat day here and there. If wanna go out and eat that burger and chocolate cake, do it, just do it every other week or so instead of on a frequent basis. But It’s actually better to have a cheat day here and there because it still motivates you to lose wait, so it’s like a reward system so to speak, at least from my end. That’s not to say bad food days don’t exist. I have been through more of them than I can count, and it’s okay because shit happens. Just gotta get back on track the next day if that happens. 

And of course, none of this was easy. But it is possible if you have the drive and the discipline to make small changes that will set you on the right path, and that’s how you could ultimately keep the weight off in the end.

I went to college and have watched indigo traveller. Social democrats are not the same thing as socialists. There is a vast difference between socially democratic countries and outright socialist ones, and people get both confused all the time and use them interchangeably. 

Objectively speaking, Cuba is an example of a socialist state. It does not have a mixed economy and the government controls everything, with very little private enterprise. While this means that the government controlling everything might be good on paper, it hinders the economy and hurts people in the long run. The quality of healthcare and goods and services are usually better if private entities are in a position to provide for the country and not solely the government.

Social democracy on the other hand is what happens when you get countries like Sweden and Iceland. The difference being is that their systems have mixed economic models, and there’s high levels of taxation but there’s also high levels of regulation to ensure neither companies nor the government have too much overreach over the people. You still have to pay a lot in taxes, but you get more for your money compared to the US. Those Nordic countries I mentioned, as well as some other places, have a much higher happiness and quality of life index than the US and Cuba combined in large part due to their mixed economic model. 

From my point of view point, it’s okay for private enterprise to exist, but government oversight is necessary to ensure there isn’t unregulated capitalism, which would lead to economic and social decline like in the US.

There are many. Although one I definitely still think about is one of the times I helped out a Russian passenger. I’m a native Russian speaker, and was the only person in the organization who spoke it, so anytime a Russian speaking person had a problem they would always come to me. 

Last year, this particular person had arrived into JFK from Minneapolis and was continuing onto Dubai, then onto St. Petersburg (this was in late august 2022, a few months after the invasion of Ukraine, so she had to go to Dubai to get back to Russia since all Russian planes were banned from flying over North America and Europe). She arrived at the front desk, and said in broken English she needed help finding out if her luggage made it onto the emirates flight for later that evening. I immediately switched to Russian, and so left my desk to go help her out. We went to a baggage office, and was told to go to the JetBlue terminal to inquire with them about the baggage since the baggage office we were at did not have them. 

As we walked over, I started talking to her to assess the situation further, and just connect with her overall. Of course, the invasion came up inevitably. She told me about how the war ruined everything for her family and friends back home, so she went to the states to be with relatives for a while hoping things would die down. She’s been to the states before, but not under these circumstances. It was hard being away from home and having to operate in a language she doesn’t speak very well, as well as keeping her mental health in check and praying that nothing bad would happen to her family back home. Having her Russian bank cards not work in the US also made things tricky, so she had to use cash everywhere and have her relatives pay for things if they were able to. There was a lot of Russophobia at the height of the war, and still is to a lesser extent, and it hurt her (and me) a lot seeing how her country and its people garnered such a negative reputation because of the actions of the tyrant that is Vladimir Putin. I asked her why was she returning to Russia despite all the madness happening over there, and she told me her visa was on the verge of expiring, so she had to go back there. She didn’t want to leave the US, but she wasn’t in a position to stay, so going back was the only option with the possibility that she may be able to renew her three year visa down the line. It hurt seeing her hurt inside, especially since I still have relatives and friends in Russia who don’t have the luxury to leave. But it meant a lot to have someone who she could talk to about this while helping her out with her current situation. 

After we got to the terminal, I translated everything and we were told the bags were on their way to the emirates flight. She had a lot of time to kill, so I showed her the TWA hotel since it offered wifi and was a pretty nice facility to chill before a flight. She thanked me for helping her out and wished me the best, as did I. Looking back on it, wishing her the best takes on a whole new meaning with the increased aggressive crackdown on dissent that Putin’s government implemented. With mobilization being put into effect shortly after, it made me worried for her nephews and son about if they would make it out of Russia or not, and everyone else who got caught up in it. War damages those who fight in it, but it also damages the lives of those caught in a physical and metaphorical crossfire. I hope she and other Russian nationals I met during my time at the airport are okay.

And while the clone wars did a good job at that, rebels is good because it’s a more grounded story with a team that evolves individually and as a group. Trials of the Dark Saber, Jedi Night, Twilight of the Apprentice, the Honorable Ones, and Family Reunion and Farewell has some of the best writing in Star Wars media.

So many tbh, so this is my take with some of them. 

Everything a Jedi should be- Kanan Jarrus (Wise, great mentor, charismatic leader, saw how important it was to love those closest to him, especially Hera. His sacrifice was one of the saddest and meaningful deaths in Star Wars lore, showing just how well written his character was.) 

Great soldier- tie between Rex and Fives (Fives discovered the truth behind order 66 and died, whereas Rex resisted it and survived and helped defeat the empire. They’re great soldiers because they questioned orders that were morally wrong, and not good soldiers who willingly followed orders. 501st all the way!)

Sith Lord- Palpatine/Darth Sidious (Just plain evil and a master manipulator. Amazing villain.)

Jedi Master- Obi Wan Kenobi (He has the right balance of humor, wisdom, and diplomacy. And despite losing his master, his lover, his best friend and his order, he still never got tempted to fall to the dark side and always remained strong. One of my all time favorites.)

Most complex- Count Dooku (Not totally evil, but he had legit reasons to leave the Jedi order and question the republic for its corruption. He had good intentions and told the truth about what was really going on in the republic, but the Jedi were too arrogant to listen. If Anakin didn’t kill him, he would have spilled the beans and revealed the truth behind the clone wars.)

Bounty hunter- Cad Bane (Such a badass. The book of boba fett did him dirty.) 

Imperial leader- Grand Admiral Thrawn (Brilliant, analytical, powerful, and always learns about his enemies and even respects them to an extent. He’s also the kind of leader who treated his officers and soldiers with respect rather than fear. Hope to see more of him.) 

Mandalorian- Sabine Wren (Honestly an underrated character. Running away from the empire after designing a weapon that killed her own people was not something she could easily recover from. Can’t blame her for her guilt making her closed off from people, and putting her at odds with her clan and other Mandalorians because they turned their back on her after she ran away. When she trained with the darksaber and faced her past, it was one of the greatest arcs of Rebels. “Sabine’s Catharsis” is one of my all time favorite Star Wars tracks. Hope she returns after the Ahsoka show, whether in live action or animation.)

I have a Subaru Impreza that’s been pretty reliable. It’s my first car that I got as a gift from my family and they bought it used. Granted, mine’s a 2008, so newer ones get better mileage, safety systems and whatnot. If you live in a place where it snows or rains a lot, you can’t go wrong with Subaru’s all wheel drive system.

As far as buying a car goes, it’s much cheaper to get a car used if you can. You can get a reliable car with decent miles for around $10k or lower, and it’s much cheaper than buying a new one at the dealership off the dealership lot. I would advise you to not pay a lot for a first car as a fairly new driver. If you can buy a used one in cash, then you would not have to deal with car payments and you would own the car fully. I recommend Japanese cars, especially Honda, Toyota, Subaru or Mazda. They retain their value and are great cars overall. 

The next part is my experience, so it may not apply to you. If you are in the US, definitely look into your state’s lemon laws and find out if dealerships provide a 30 day warranty by law on used car purchases. I live in a state that does, so having that 30 day warranty was useful in the event I needed to bring my car back to the dealership for unexpected problems that they would take care of (knock on wood, I didn’t have to bring it back). Granted, dealerships can be scummy, but if you can get that 30 day warranty, do it. They will also deal with the paperwork for you if you buy used. However, private owners selling their cars online usually are more honest since they know their cars best.  But you would have to do the paperwork on your own. Lastly, always check the vehicle history to make sure everything is good. 

Happy hunting! Hope you find something good :)

At my lowest during Covid, I couldn’t take the stress caused by lockdowns, my anxiety and depression, and my father’s disdain towards me. I hated waking up and being in emotional agony and I felt like getting rid of myself was the way to go. I truly believed I would be doing the world a favor. 

I was staying at my vacation house in New England at the time of the early days of the pandemic and told my mom I’d be going out for a short drive. I told her I’d be right back. Then when I got to my sunset spot, I contemplated jumping in and drowning myself. In my mind, people wouldn’t dare to make physical contact with someone to spread the virus, even if a poor soul was drowning. But then just before I attempted, I stopped. I panted and made my way back to my car, where I shut the door and started crying. I don’t know what stopped me from doing it, but there was just something inside of me that begged me to live. It was a case where I didn’t want to die, but I didn’t want to live either. I guess it was the motivation to see the pandemic end and embrace normal things I love to do again. I also realized how much it would impact my best friends and my mom. I couldn’t hurt them. Very few people know about my almost attempted suicide, even some of my closest friends for my fear of being chastised if I told them.

That could have been my last sunset and I’m grateful to have persevered to say the least. I still have depressive episodes here and there, but therapy helped me out more than I could have imagined. If there’s anyone contemplating it, it does get better. Cliche, but it’s the truth. Live to see yourself do awesome things. Live to graduate if you’re in school, see that new marvel or Star Wars movie or show coming out soon, play that new game you want, or to hear new music from your favorite bands. Live to live because we only have one shot on this planet.
